newsitem.title: UK: INSIGHT-Drop in Scottish banks seen.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT-Drop in Scottish banks seen.

text.p: Shares in Royal Bank of Scotland and Bank of Scotland are poised to fall to fresh lows for the year, even as the rest of the UK bank sector seems certain to outperform the broad market, technical analysts said.
"Banks as a whole looked good for a while, but it's not that nice, neat homogeneous sector any more. The Scotish banks broke down," said Robin Griffiths, an analyst with HSBC James Capel.
He is bullish on the other major British banks, but has a sell recommendation on both Royal Bank of Scotland and Bank of Scotland.
Technical indicators point to a steep decline the shares in of both Scotish banks, which have lagged the market all year.
Royal Bank of Scotland shares were down 1/2p to 486-1/2p at 1200 GMT, are only about 20p from their lows for the year, and momentum indicators portend a drop below that level.
Chartwatchers noted the 200-day moving average, a closely watched momentum indicator, crossed share prices in early June and have traded below the average since.
"Now the 200-day moving average is turning (downward) and that means the trend is lower," said analyst David Charters of Investment Research of Cambridge.
Royal Bank of Scotland shares peaked in mid-December at 658p. The shares have been slipping since, even as the UK bank sector shot ahead, leading blue chips into unchartered territory.
Charters said Royal Bank of Scotland shares look set to test critical support at 460p, a level not seen in almost a year.
If chart support at 460p is breached, Charters, who also rates the stock a sell, forecasts a further decline to 400p.
"If 460p goes, then I'd say we'll see 400p in three to six months," he said. "The other mainstream banks look okay ... they look good," Charters added.
Shares in the Bank of Scotland, down 1p to 255p, also have traded below their 200-day moving average since early June. Those shares could fall as low as 200p, said Griffiths.
"That's major support ... falling to 200p would retrace its entire '95 rise," he added.
